claim.pdf_says:
25) The STEP phrase shall be specified if the entry:
    a) contains an absolute LINE clause, or
    b) has an entry with an absolute LINE clause subordinate to it, or
    c) contains an absolute COLUMN clause, or
[page 462 ends here; page 463 opens with]
    d) is subordinate to an entry with a LINE clause and has an entry with an absolute COLUMN clause subordinate to it.

    In all other cases, the STEP phrase is optional.
claim.markdown_says: c) contains an absolute COLUMN clause, or d) is subordinate to an entry with a LINE clause and has an entry with an absolute COLUMN clause subordinate to it. ## Page 463 **ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)** In all other cases, the STEP phrase is optional.
claim.why_it_matters: Sub-item d) of 13.18.38.3 GR 25 (OCCURS clause, FORMAT 3, when the STEP phrase is mandatory) is printed as its own list item at the top of PDF page 463, but the markdown runs it into the tail of item c) on page 462, so the enumeration ends at c) and d) survives only as an unlabelled clause hanging off c) after the word 'or'. Four independent conditions become three, one of them a garbled compound; a reader or extractor enumerating the mandatory-STEP conditions loses d) as a distinct condition, and the page attribution of d) is wrong (462 instead of 463).

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on two independent grounds: the claim misquotes the markdown, and the only genuine difference is page-break/paragraph formatting with zero content loss.

WHAT THE PDF GLYPHS ACTUALLY SHOW. Rendered page 462 at 300 dpi (E:/Temp/specrecon/v462/spec_p462.png, printed folio 432): GR 25 reads 'The STEP phrase shall be specified if the entry:' followed by three separately indented, blank-line-separated items whose printed choice indicators are the glyphs 'a)', 'b)', 'c)' -- 'a)  contains an absolute LINE clause, or' / 'b)  has an entry with an absolute LINE clause subordinate to it, or' / 'c)  contains an absolute COLUMN clause, or'. The page then ends (footer '432  (c)ISO/IEC 2023'). Rendered page 463 (E:/Temp/specrecon/v463/spec_p463.png, printed folio 433) opens with the glyph 'd)' at the same indent: 'd)  is subordinate to an entry with a LINE clause and has an entry with an absolute COLUMN clause subordinate to it.', then the flush paragraph 'In all other cases, the STEP phrase is optional.' So the claim's rendering of the PDF is accurate.

WHAT THE MARKDOWN ACTUALLY SAYS. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 19671 (verified directly in the canonical file, not only in the extracted work unit) reads verbatim: 'c) contains an absolute COLUMN clause, or d) is subordinate to an entry with a LINE clause and has an entry with an absolute COLUMN clause subordinate to it.' The choice indicator 'd)' IS PRESENT, literally, in the transcription. Lines 19665-19671 carry all four labels a), b), c), d) and the full text of every one of the four conditions, word for word identical to the PDF. Line 19673-19675 open page 463, and line 19677-area carries 'In all other cases, the STEP phrase is optional.' -- matching the PDF exactly.

WHY THE CLAIM FAILS. (1) MISQUOTE / FALSE PREMISE: the claim asserts 'the enumeration ends at c)' and that 'd) survives only as an unlabelled clause hanging off c) after the word or'. Both are false -- 'd)' is spelled out as a labelled choice indicator in the markdown. Consequently 'Four independent conditions become three, one of them a garbled compound' is also false: four labelled conditions remain four labelled conditions, with identical text. Any extractor keying on the printed choice indicators (the natural way to enumerate an ISO sub-list) finds a), b), c) and d). (2) FORMATTING/PAGE-BREAK FURNITURE ONLY: the sole real difference is that the blank line the transcription normally places between sub-items is absent between c) and d), because the OCR pipeline joined the last line of page 462 to the first line of page 463 across the page boundary -- the classic reflow-across-a-page-break artifact. That also explains the 'page attribution' point: d) sits inside the page-462 block rather than the page-463 block. Attaching a continuation to the page where its enclosing rule began is page-break furniture, not a content discrepancy; no citation, section number, rule number, condition, or word of normative text is altered, dropped, duplicated, or reordered. Rule 25's meaning -- STEP is mandatory under exactly these four conditions, optional otherwise -- is fully and correctly recoverable from the markdown.

No normative content is missing or changed, so this does not rise to a structural discrepancy. At most it is a cosmetic tidy-up (insert a paragraph break before 'd)' and move it below the page-463 anchor) that a transcription-hygiene pass could make, and it should not be logged as a spec-reconciliation defect.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. Item d) of 13.18.38.3 GR 25 is present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md (line 19671) complete with its literal 'd)' choice indicator and its full verbatim text; the claim's assertion that d) is 'unlabelled' and that 'the enumeration ends at c)' misquotes the markdown. The only actual difference is cosmetic page-break furniture: the OCR joined the last line of PDF page 462 ('c) ... or') to the first line of PDF page 463 ('d) ...'), so the usual blank line between sub-items is missing and d) is filed under the page-462 anchor instead of page-463. All four conditions, their labels, and 'In all other cases, the STEP phrase is optional.' are transcribed correctly and the rule's meaning is unchanged. Optional hygiene only: insert a paragraph break before 'd)' and relocate it beneath the page-463 anchor.
